Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

You can think of this conversion setup as a web of relationships, with your local MyCtx type as its root. A handy way to picture it is a bunch of grapes, where MyCtx is the stem. Once you grab that stem, it doesn't matter how many third-party types hang off it (Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and so on). You lift the whole bunch at once, and the compiler accepts all of them as local implementations.Better yet, you can define more than one stem in the same project. For instance, your HTTP API layer can use ApiCtx to format timestamps as strings, while an internal RPC layer uses RpcCtx to format them as integer timestamps. Both sets of rules live under separate contexts, completely isolated at compile time, with zero conflict.One detail to watch out for: the local type has to be a real, newly defined type. Creating a type alias for a foreign type will not work.The Position of the Local Type MattersAt this point, you might think that dropping a local type MyCtx anywhere into a trait's generic list solves the Orphan Rule for good. Most of the time, it does. But if your trait has more than one generic parameter, or if you want to write a generic impl, there is an ordering restriction that is easy to trip over.When the compiler runs its Orphan Rule check, it scans the types in a fixed order: first the Self type, then the trait's 1st generic parameter, then the 2nd, and so on. The rule comes down to one sentence: no bare generic type parameter T may appear before the first local type.Code makes this clearest. Suppose an external crate defines ForeignTrait and ForeignType, and you define MyCtx locally:// ✅ Allowed: scans ForeignType, then hits local MyCtx first; the trailing T is unrestricted impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T before seeing MyCtx impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T right away in Self, before MyCtx gets a chance impl ForeignTrait for T {}The only word to pay attention to here is "bare". In Rust terminology, this is called an uncovered type parameter. A plain T is uncovered. If it is wrapped inside a non-fundamental concrete type like Vec (built-in fundamental types like &T and Box do not count), it is no longer uncovered, so it will not block a local MyCtx that comes after it:// ✅ Allowed: T is covered by Vec, so it is not an uncovered type parameter impl ForeignTrait, MyCtx> for ForeignType {}From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position. That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors.A Truly Standalone models CrateOnce this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases.As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate.Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid, Url, and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models, you are left with two bad options:Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models, and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace.Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows.With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types:// crate: models pub struct Product { pub id: uuid::Uuid, pub created_at: chrono::DateTime, }Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

At this point, you might think that dropping a local type MyCtx anywhere into a trait's generic list solves the Orphan Rule for good. Most of the time, it does. But if your trait has more than one generic parameter, or if you want to write a generic impl, there is an ordering restriction that is easy to trip over.When the compiler runs its Orphan Rule check, it scans the types in a fixed order: first the Self type, then the trait's 1st generic parameter, then the 2nd, and so on. The rule comes down to one sentence: no bare generic type parameter T may appear before the first local type.Code makes this clearest. Suppose an external crate defines ForeignTrait and ForeignType, and you define MyCtx locally:// ✅ Allowed: scans ForeignType, then hits local MyCtx first; the trailing T is unrestricted impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T before seeing MyCtx impl ForeignTrait for ForeignType {} // ❌ Error: hits a bare T right away in Self, before MyCtx gets a chance impl ForeignTrait for T {}The only word to pay attention to here is "bare". In Rust terminology, this is called an uncovered type parameter. A plain T is uncovered. If it is wrapped inside a non-fundamental concrete type like Vec (built-in fundamental types like &T and Box do not count), it is no longer uncovered, so it will not block a local MyCtx that comes after it:// ✅ Allowed: T is covered by Vec, so it is not an uncovered type parameter impl ForeignTrait, MyCtx> for ForeignType {}From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position. That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors.A Truly Standalone models CrateOnce this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases.As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate.Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid, Url, and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models, you are left with two bad options:Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models, and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace.Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows.With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types:// crate: models pub struct Product { pub id: uuid::Uuid, pub created_at: chrono::DateTime, }Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project?When building my own Rust ORM, Kova, I applied this pattern across the entire type system. It is a good concrete example of how this plays out in practice.ORMs are where the Orphan Rule hurts the most. A single table often mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types. Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

From a library author's perspective, this means it is not enough to just add a generic slot; you also need to put it in the right place. If your trait has multiple generic parameters and there is no strong reason otherwise, put the context Ctx in the first type parameter position. That way, downstream users writing generic implementations can avoid most of the surprising Orphan Rule errors.A Truly Standalone models CrateOnce this mechanism clicks, you will see that it also solves a stubborn architectural headache in larger Rust codebases.As a project grows, it usually gets split into a Cargo workspace: maybe an API gateway crate, a few business service crates, and a background worker crate. These modules often share the same data structures, so the natural move is to pull those structs out into a standalone models crate.Traditionally, doing this in Rust is painful. Suppose models defines a Product struct with Uuid, Url, and DateTime fields. If your serialization library or ORM expects those field types to already implement its traits inside models, you are left with two bad options:Wrap everything in NewTypes inside models, and pull in the serialization library, database driver, and other heavy dependencies along with them. A crate that was supposed to hold plain data structures ends up with the heaviest dependency tree in the workspace.Give up on splitting it out, and dump models and business logic into the same crate. It saves time early on, but dependency boundaries and compile times get harder to manage as the project grows.With the generic Ctx parameter, that knot comes untied. Inside your standalone models crate, you just define your structs with native types:// crate: models pub struct Product { pub id: uuid::Uuid, pub created_at: chrono::DateTime, }Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Does this idea still hold up when you bring it into a real, more complex project?When building my own Rust ORM, Kova, I applied this pattern across the entire type system. It is a good concrete example of how this plays out in practice.ORMs are where the Orphan Rule hurts the most. A single table often mixes Uuid, Url, DateTime, HashMap, and custom domain types. Kova's core Encode and Decode traits use the exact generic slot design we just walked through:pub trait Encode<'a, X = ()> { fn encode(self) -> Result>; } pub trait Decode: Sized { fn decode(value: Value<'_>) -> Result; }Because Kova hands the extension point to the user, it only needs built-in support for basic database primitives: integers, floats, booleans, strings, and byte arrays. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

Then you write a generic implementation for Product open to any Ctx (or let a derive macro generate it):impl ToJson for Product where uuid::Uuid: ToJson, chrono::DateTime: ToJson { fn to_json(&self) -> String { format!( "{{\"id\":{},\"created_at\":{}}}", ToJson::::to_json(&self.id), ToJson::::to_json(&self.created_at), ) } }Notice the subtle part here: inside the models crate, Uuid and DateTime do not implement ToJson yet, and this code still compiles.That is because models is only declaring a deferred contract: "whoever uses this later, as long as your context Ctx knows how to handle Uuid and DateTime, Product automatically supports ToJson under your context." As a result, models stays completely lightweight, carries no concrete conversion logic, and compiles very fast. The actual conversions are deferred to the downstream service crates, where each service hooks up what it needs using its own local context.For large workspaces, this keeps dependency boundaries clean. Models can evolve on their own, while different services remain free to pick whatever storage format or API representation they need.Real-World Example: How This Works in KovaThe ToJson snippet above is as minimal as it gets. Its Cargo.toml does not have to maintain a pile of optional dependencies and feature flags for uuid, chrono, jiff, url, and so on.In a real application, the workflow looks just like the earlier example.First, define your table structs with native types in a standalone models crate and add #[derive(Model)]:// crate: models (no database driver or codec code needed) #[derive(Model)] pub struct Product { pub id: Uuid, pub price: Decimal, pub vendor_url: Url, pub created_at: DateTime, }#[derive(Model)] expands into an open contract like impl Model for Product where ..., so models compiles completely on its own without tying itself to any concrete codec implementation.Next, in your downstream service crate, define a local marker struct pub struct AppCodec; and implement zero-copy conversions matching your storage layout:pub struct AppCodec; // Store Uuid as 16 raw bytes, borrowing directly with zero copies impl<'a, 'b: 'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for &'b Uuid { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Blob(Cow::Borrowed(self.as_bytes()))) } } // Store DateTime as an integer millisecond timestamp impl<'a> Encode<'a, AppCodec> for DateTime { fn encode(self) -> Result> { Ok(Value::Int8(self.timestamp_millis())) } }Finally, switch the client's context marker when you need it:// Default client using the () codec let client = Options::from(conn_str).build()?; // Switch to the local AppCodec at zero runtime cost let client = client.codec::();Switching the type carries zero runtime overhead; under the hood, it only swaps a PhantomData marker on Client from () to AppCodec. And while building Kova, another nice benefit showed up: once you have a local type like AppCodec, you can attach much more to it than just encoding and decoding.For example, suppose you have implemented Encode for url::Url in an ORM. If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

If you still can't run LIKE queries on a Url column, or compare a Url column directly against a &str, that type still feels second-class in queries.So Kova puts the same generic extension slot on its SQL capability traits and type compatibility rules, such as CanString, CanMath, and Compatible. Users can add a couple of short declarations under their own AppCodec:// Give Url string capabilities (enabling methods like `like` and `ilike`) impl CanString for Url {} // Allow passing &str directly to a Url column without calling Url::parse() every time impl<'a> Compatible, AppCodec> for Static<&'a str> {}With that in place, third-party types fit right into the ORM's DSL and behave no differently from built-in types:client .update::() .set(Product::vendor_url.set("https://rust-lang.org")) .filter(Product::id.eq(&target_uuid) & Product::vendor_url.ilike("https://%")) .execute() .await?;Putting this design through a real codebase like Kova confirmed something practical: opening up type conversions and capabilities to a user-defined context does more than just get around the Orphan Rule on paper. Even in a complex framework, it keeps dependency boundaries clean, compile times fast, and day-to-day usage comfortable.Rust's Orphan Rule is not there to make life hard. It exists to prevent global implementation conflicts and stop crates from stepping on each other in the global namespace. Once you stop fighting for a "globally unique" implementation and instead leave a generic slot on the trait to scope uniqueness to a local context, bypassing the Orphan Rule takes no black magic at all. It is just a simple shift in perspective, yet it makes both library design and large workspace boundaries much cleaner.In the next post, I will walk through the problem that immediately follows this design: once your traits and builders carry a generic context parameter, how do you keep them from spiraling into nested generic types and slow compile times? That brings us to boundary validation and type erasure.(The patterns in this series come from Kova, a macro-free PostgreSQL and SQLite ORM for Rust. If you want to see how the full type system fits together, check out the source and docs on GitHub.)

#9847. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9846. UK MPs want AI watchdog with power to pull the plug on dangerous models

Parliamentary committee says tech giants can't be left to mark their own homework when it comes to AI safety

UK MPs want a watchdog with the power to pull the plug on dangerous AI models, rather than leave the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic to decide when they've gone too far.

In a report shared with The Register ahead of publication on Wednesday, a parliamentary committee is calling for an AI Safety and Security Bill that would give a watchdog powers to intervene while models are still being developed.

It could halt high-risk training and testing, block deployments, or suspend AI services if the risks can't be contained. LLMs are trained on billions of learned parameters and so developers can't always predict what a model will do in every situation.

The recommendations come from Parliament's Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee, which questioned researchers, former AI employees, and representatives from OpenAI, Google DeepMind, Anthropic, and Meta.

All four companies assured MPs they wouldn't release models they considered unsafe. The trouble is, they don't use the same yardstick for safety, and UK law doesn't generally require them to get an independent opinion before releasing anything.

"We cannot give today’s AI leaders unfettered freedom to behave like modern-day Dr Frankensteins, creating dangers beyond anyone’s control," said committee chair Liam Byrne MP.

Just as with aviation, pharma or nuclear safety, UK government want to rely on manufacturers' assurance alone, and want regulation.

"Our hearings exposed gaps in independent scrutiny, incident reporting and powers to stop unsafe systems. Once some models are released, they cannot reliably be recalled," added Byrne. "Protection must begin while systems are being built and tested."

The committee's report, Guardrails for Growth: Making AI Safe, identifies ten holes in Britain's approach to AI safety, including the lack of mandatory incident reporting, limited access for independent testers, and inadequate protections for whistleblowers.

The UK already has an AI Security Institute (AISI), which has made a name for itself testing some of the world's most powerful models, but its work depends on voluntary cooperation, and it has no authority to stop a company releasing a model that raises safety concerns.

MPs want AISI to continue its testing work while a separate regulator takes responsibility for enforcement. Developers of designated high-risk systems would have to provide evidence supporting their safety claims and give independent researchers access to examine them. Significant changes to a model's capabilities or safeguards would trigger further scrutiny.

Former AI employees also told MPs that raising safety concerns can come at a price. Restrictive contracts, commercial pressures, and financial disincentives can all discourage staff from speaking out, the committee heard. MPs want stronger legal protections for whistleblowers and compulsory reporting of AI incidents and near misses.

There's a fair bit of money riding on this, too. Using OECD productivity estimates, the committee calculates that AI could leave Britain's economy up to £400 billion larger over the next decade. It also sees an opportunity for the UK to make money from independently testing AI models, building on the expertise already established at AISI. MPs argue that stronger safeguards could encourage businesses, particularly smaller firms, to adopt the technology.

"AI firms must be required to substantiate their safety claims, independent experts must be able to scrutinize them, and a regulator must have the power to intervene when risks cannot be controlled," Byrne said. "Ministers, accountable to Parliament, must decide what risks the public should be asked to bear."

MPs want the new laws on the books in the next parliamentary session, and say Britain should use its turn at the G20 helm in 2027 to get other countries on board with tougher rules for AI testing, incident reporting, and risky model releases.

Whether ministers are prepared to hand a watchdog the power to stop AI development is another matter. The committee's recommendations aren't binding, and the government has yet to commit to the proposed legislation. ®

#9845. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

The lexical fallback for scale-to-zero and the separate index activation boundary are useful production details. One question for the hybrid setup: do you measure relevance and latency separately when dense search is cold versus warm, so fallback quality is visible rather than hidden in an overall average? We examined lexical-first retrieval and semantic reranking on a smaller workload here: https://huggingface.co/blog/ironbcc/bm25-seb-rag-retrieval (I'm an author). That benchmark doesn't establish behavior on a paper-scale corpus.

#9843. Energy-Based Reasoners: Your Recurrent Reasoner Should Be an Energy-Based Model

TL;DR – We introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), reasoning models that learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. Its value scores candidate predictions without requiring an external verifier, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a natural signal for stopping. With only 1.8M parameters, EBRs achieve 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model. On N-Queens and Graph Coloring, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy.

Looping is a powerful inductive bias for reasoning. By repeatedly iterating a recurrent block, looped models can scale their effective depth and enable multi-step reasoning in latent space. However, existing looped models are not inherently guided by an explicit measure of progress, making it difficult to determine when to stop looping and how to improve upon the current state. To enable this, we introduce Energy-Based Reasoners (EBRs), which learn an energy function over latent reasoning states and formulate looped updates as gradient descent on this energy. The energy scores latent states, while its gradient guides refinement and provides a signal for stopping. To train EBRs effectively, we further introduce exploration-based training to discover additional modes and to better shape the energy landscape over a broader set of states. Across four algorithmic reasoning benchmarks, EBRs match or outperform prior recurrent reasoning models, achieving 99.9% accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme while using 345× less inference compute than the next-best model and maintaining comparable training compute. On all multi-solution benchmarks, EBRs achieve state-of-the-art coverage of distinct valid solutions while maintaining near-100% single-sample accuracy. These results suggest that energy-based models are a promising approach for strong reasoning performance.

Existing looped reasoners update their latent state without any explicit assessment of it. An EBR learns an energy function that guides refinement, stopping and selection.

Score. The energy rates the compatibility between the reasoning state z and the initial board x. Lower means better compatibility.

Refine. The gradient turns the score into an improvement direction.

Stop. The state becomes stationary once the gradient is small, so the gradient acts as a stopping criterion.

Select. Among multiple candidate solutions, we pick the one with the lowest energy.

Correct solutions settle at low-energy stationary states. Energy, gradient norm and step size during descent on Sudoku-Extreme. Correct trajectories settle at low energy with small gradients, while wrong ones keep moving.

Running more descent steps refines each answer further, and running more trajectories gives the energy more candidates to choose the lowest-energy one from.

EBRs reach EqR's best accuracy with 7× fewer iterations (left) and 43× fewer samples (right).

GRAM and TRM from GRAM's paper; EqR from its released checkpoint. Mean ± SD over three seeds.

Each trajectory stops once its energy gradient falls below a threshold, so easy puzzles finish in a few steps and hard ones keep going.

EBRs give the best single-sample accuracy among reasoning models. Within only 5 passes, they reach 99.9% and 88.3%, ahead of methods that draw up to 128. Stopping each trajectory once its energy gradient falls below a threshold keeps 99.9% accuracy with 10.9× fewer FLOPs than a fixed-depth EBR, allowing us to surpass EqR with 345× fewer FLOPs.

EBR acts like stochastic gradient descent and can capture many different solutions. Coverage captures the share of each input's distinct valid solutions that 20 samples find.

Pass@1 (%) and Conflicts (edges summed over the test graphs) use one sample. Cov@20 is the share of distinct valid solutions found by 20 samples (%). Baselines from GRAM's paper.

InfoQ Homepage Presentations Scaling LLM-Based Ranking Systems for Latency-Critical Search & Recommendation Workloads

Sundara Raman Ramachandran shares how LinkedIn productionizes LLM ranking under strict P99 latency SLAs. He discusses distilling a 7B model down to 400M parameters, compressing job contexts into single-token embeddings for a 10x throughput leap, and eliminating hidden system bottlenecks - from custom flash attention masks to Python GIL workarounds, gc.freeze, and non-blocking CUDA memory copies.

Sundara Raman Ramachandran is a Lead Engineer on LinkedIn’s LLM Inference team, where he plays a key role in designing and scaling the infrastructure powering LLM-based ranking systems for search and recommendation. His work centers on building latency-critical, high-throughput LLM serving platforms that operate reliably at global scale.

QCon AI is a practitioner-led event focused entirely on the engineering discipline required to scale these workloads safely. It provides direct access to the architectural playbooks and failure metrics that peer organizations use in production.

Presented by: David Iparraguirre - Senior Product Marketing Manager at Datadog, and Jessica Yang - Product Manager at Datadog

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

Sundara Raman Ramachandran: I'm Sundara. I'm a tech lead at LinkedIn. My current focus is on LLM inference and using LLMs for ranking and recommendation workloads. I'm also an open-source contributor in SGLang where I have primarily contributed to the scoring API where we use LLMs for ranking. I have close to 10 years of industry experience. I have worked with Microsoft in different products like Microsoft Office and Azure. Today I'm going to talk about how we scale the LLM based ranking systems at LinkedIn, what were the challenges we encountered, and what are some learnings and takeaways you can take from the talk.

I hope all of you would have used LinkedIn at some point, that you might have used it for searching for some job or you're looking for someone in a network. The reason I ask is LinkedIn Search operates at a massive scale. If you haven't read it already, maybe after the talk you can take up the LinkedIn app and maybe search about me. In LinkedIn's use case, you might be searching for a job where you enter, find me design roles in the entertainment industry.
